claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Slow cooling permits sufficient diffusion for Al, and to a lesser extent Cr, to segregate and locally order.
Al and Cr segregation and local ordering trigger nucleation of ordered secondary phases such as B2.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion-driven formation of ordered secondary phases.
Cooling rate should be varied by comparing rapidly quenched and slowly cooled samples originating from the same high-temperature BCC state.
Isothermal aging at a temperature where diffusion is active will further evolve ordered phases.
Diffusion and segregation of Al and Cr promote an ordered secondary phase within the matrix.
Al has sufficient mobility during slow cooling to segregate into compositionally distinct localized regions.
Local Al enrichment favors an ordering transition from disordered BCC to a B2-type structure.
Rapid quenching largely retains the high-temperature BCC phase.
After identical thermal exposure, quenched samples will be less affected than slow-cooled samples because they lack sufficient initial ordering nuclei.
The slow-cooled and subsequently aged sample will have a significantly higher ordered-phase fraction than the quenched baseline.
The rapidly quenched baseline will remain predominantly BCC with minimal diffusion-mediated ordering.
The mechanism should apply when cooling is sufficiently slow to permit elemental diffusion and ordering.
The mechanism should not apply during extremely rapid cooling or when diffusion is inhibited by low exposure temperature or very short aging time.
A lack of statistically significant enhancement of ordered phases in slow-cooled and aged samples relative to quenched and aged samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.
